title: Only 10% Can Pass This Grammar Quiz
summary: Broken sentences, punctuation traps and almost-correct wording test whether any mistake can slip past you.

landing.intro: Think your grammar is flawless? Repair broken sentences, catch tiny punctuation traps and prove you can spot the mistake before it catches you.

about.body:
This worldwide-English challenge contains ten carefully varied questions on sentence structure, punctuation, tense, pronouns, reference clarity and precise editing. Each item is written specifically for English rather than translated from another language.

Choose the one answer that makes the sentence correct and natural in its stated context. Correctness remains hidden until the final reveal.

Your score reflects this short language challenge only. It is not a formal literacy assessment or educational qualification.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Complete ten carefully selected questions in one focused challenge.
Choose one answer each time. Correctness remains hidden until the final reveal.
Reveal your result, skill breakdown and complete answer review after the final question.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment, academic qualification or proof of language proficiency.

checkpoint.finalAdNote: One short ad, then your results.

stage-1.preAdCopy: Your grammar score and three-skill breakdown are ready to reveal.

profile-1.title: The Master Editor
profile-1.copy: You handled structure, reference and tiny punctuation details with exceptional control. Even the final multi-clue edits rarely disturbed your command of the page.

profile-2.title: The Natural Grammarian
profile-2.copy: You recognised how sentences fit together and caught most of the challenge’s nearly invisible errors. Your judgement stayed reliable as the material moved from isolated lines to real editing contexts.

profile-3.title: The Sentence Specialist
profile-3.copy: You solved a strong majority of the proofreading problems and adapted well when the format changed. A few fine distinctions kept the final result interesting.

profile-4.title: The Careful Communicator
profile-4.copy: You have a dependable grasp of everyday grammar and a clear eye for several important editing patterns. Your strongest skill shows where that language instinct becomes most confident.

profile-5.title: The Language Improver
profile-5.copy: You caught a solid share of the errors and kept adjusting as the challenge became more demanding. The review will show which patterns are ready to become second nature.

profile-6.title: The Grammar Detective
profile-6.copy: The challenge found some well-hidden traps, but it also revealed the language clues you already notice naturally. Every missed answer is a useful pattern to recognise next time.

insights.overview: Your grammar score at a glance

grammar-r1q1.question: Which option is a complete sentence?
answers: After the final paragraph
The editor checked the final paragraph.
Because the deadline changed
While everyone was waiting

grammar-r1q3.context: The notes belong to several students.
grammar-r1q3.question: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
answers: The students’ notes were organised.
The student’s notes were organised.
The students notes’ were organised.
The students note’s were organised.

grammar-r3q1.question: The meeting began at 09:00. Leo finished the chart at 08:30. Which sentence is correct?
answers: Leo completed the chart after the meeting began.
Leo had completed the chart after the meeting began.
Leo has completed the chart before the meeting began.
Leo had completed the chart before the meeting began.

grammar-r4q3.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
answers: The file was large; because it loaded slowly.
The file was large; it loaded slowly.
The file was large, it loaded slowly.
The file was large; although it loaded slowly.

grammar-r5q4.context: Between Lina and ___, this decision must remain confidential.
grammar-r5q4.question: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence?
answers: me
I
my
mine

grammar-r5q6.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a direct address?
answers: Ravi please, check the final line.
Ravi, please check the final line.
Ravi please check, the final line.
Ravi; please, check the final line.

grammar-r7q6.context: A report contains a summary and an appendix. The appendix is updated monthly.
grammar-r7q6.question: Which edit makes the monthly update refer to the appendix?
answers: The report contains a summary and an appendix, and it is updated monthly.
It contains a summary and an appendix that is updated monthly by it.
The report contains a summary and an appendix; the appendix is updated monthly.
The report, updated monthly, contains a summary and its appendix.

grammar-r9q1.question: Which sentence handles the contrast correctly?
answers: The storm ended; although the streets remained flooded.
The storm ended, however the streets remained flooded.
Although the storm ended; the streets remained flooded.
Although the storm ended, the streets remained flooded.
trapdoorErrors: semicolon incorrectly separates a main clause from a dependent clause
conjunctive adverb lacks the required boundary punctuation
semicolon incorrectly follows a dependent clause

grammar-r10q6.question: Which sentence is completely correct?
answers: After reviewing the figures, Maya confirmed that each total was accurate.
After reviewing the figures, each total was confirmed by Maya.
After reviewing the figures Maya confirmed that each total was accurate.
After reviewing the figures, Maya confirmed that each of the totals were accurate.
